decisions.quote: The number of correctly solved problems was entered into an ANOVA with prime as the independent variable. The analysis revealed no effect of prime, F(1, 86) = .08, p = .77. There was little difference between the prime conditions (action M = 11.33, SD = 3.84 vs. inaction M = 11.57, SD = 3.86). The result is shown in Figure 1. The current study failed to replicate the finding of the original study. The action and inaction primes did not produce different levels of cognitive output

decisions.quote: 1 Replication of Experiment 5 by Albarracín et al. (2008, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 95, 510-523) Seung Kyung Kim Key Jung Lee skim2@stanford.edu keyjlee@stanford.edu Introduction The original paper by Albarracín et al. (2008) tested the hypothesis that general action and inaction goals can influence the amount of motor or cognitive output of various kinds. The authors conducted a series of experiments examining the effects of instilling general action and inaction goals using word primes, such as “action” and “rest.” We plan to replicate Experiment 5, which examined the effect of action and inaction primes on cognitive output.

decisions.quote: Summary of Replication Attempt Our replication attempt of Experiment 7 of Albarracín et al. (2008) did not replicate the key results reported in the original study, suggesting that action and inaction priming had no significant influence on the number of thoughts reported. An additional analysis did not find a significant difference in the number of thoughts reported by vegetarians/vegans in comparison to non-vegetarians/non-vegans. 5 References Albarracín, D., Handley, I. M., Noguchi, K., McCulloch, K.C., Li, H., Leeper, J., Brown, R. D., Earl, A., & Hart, W. P. (2008). Increasing and decreasing motor and cognitive output: A model of general action and inaction goals. decisions.quote: A 3 (prime: action, inaction, or control) x 2 (task: active vs. inactive) factorial ANOVA design showed no significant effects of prime, F(2, 99) = .048, p = .953 (ηp2 = .001), and task, F(1, 99) = .107, p = .745 (ηp2 < .001), nor was there a significant interaction between prime and task F(2, 99) = 2.532, p = .085 (ηp2 = .049).

decisions.reason: Addressing the parent pairing flags (competing_supported_matches; same_author_year_siblings, identity_resolved=False): shipped row 1698 represents the in-lab replication of Experiment 7 of Albarracín et al. (2008, DOI 10.1037/a0012833) by Sonnleitner & Voracek (Study Num 50), while sibling row 1697 represents the online replication of Experiment 5 by Kim & Lee (Study Num 49); blind target 32 combines both into one paper-level entry. In Experiment 7, neither the focal prime x task interaction (F(2, 99) = 2.532, p = .085) nor the main effects of prime or task were significant, and the authors explicitly conclude that their attempt 'did not replicate the key results reported in the original study.' Since Experiment 5 also failed to replicate (F(1, 86) = .08, p = .77), both the experiment-specific and overall paper-level replication outcome are 'failed'.

decisions.quote: In the present replication, we focused on the final prediction in the research of Albarracín et al. Specifically, we aimed to replicate Experiment 7. In this experiment, the researchers primed participants with “action, control, or inaction words and then engaged in a brief randomly assigned task that could be either active (doodling) or inactive (resting). After the task, participants read a text and wrote down their thoughts about it” (Albarracín et al., 2008, p. 518).

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The main aim of this study was to test whether an interaction between PM cue dimension and compatibility would predict the mean proportion of missed PM cues, in a three-way mixed ANOVA including also ongoing task as a between-subjects factor. This result was partially replicated: the interaction between PM cue dimension and compatibility was strongly significant, however it was qualified by a three-way interaction with ongoing task, revealing that the effect was present only for participants in the location task condition but not for participants in the direction task condition. Also several, but not all, secondary results were successfully replicated and in addition some effects that were not present in the original paper resulted significant in this study (this might be partly due to the bigger sample size, and henceforth greater power, of this study, N=95, compared to the original study, N=40). Commentary As summarized above, the key result was partially replicated.
decisions.location: Primary Project Report 93 (https://osf.io/download/pnius/, Perugini & Costantini, Replication of Goschke & Dreisbach, 2008), Discussion - Summary of Replication Attempt and Commentary, view line 1019 (chunk 1016)
decisions.reason: In the primary replication report for Goschke & Dreisbach (2008, Psychological Science, 19, 25-32, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02042.x), the confirmatory 2 x 2 x 2 mixed ANOVA yielded a significant two-way interaction between PM cue dimension and compatibility (F(1, 93) = 18.94, p < .001), but in that same confirmatory model the effect was qualified by a significant three-way interaction with ongoing task (F(1, 93) = 12.22, p < .001), showing that the focal two-way interaction held only in the location task condition (F(1, 48) = 37.19, p < .001) and not in the direction task condition (F(1, 45) = .31, p = .582). In both the Summary of Replication Attempt and Commentary, the replicating authors explicitly conclude that 'This result was partially replicated,' that 'several, but not all, secondary results were successfully replicated,' and that 'the results are inconclusive concerning the underlying theoretical explanation.' Shipped coding ('successful') relied on the binary summary sheet column for the isolated 2-way F-test (and quoted the original effect description rather than an outcome verdict). Under the codebook rules—where confirmation of one test is not confused with the overall verdict and findings explicitly described by the authors as 'partially replicated' because they hold only in a subset of conditions are coded as 'mixed'—blind coding ('mixed') is right.
